message.content: {"vote":"keep","learning_quality_score":9,"vote_reasoning":"This question requires more than recall — it asks implementers to translate normative MUST/SHOULD guidance into concrete trust-boundary designs (consent flows, human-in-the-loop, validation, rate-limiting, sensitive-data handling, and error semantics). Answering correctly demonstrates understanding of why those controls exist, how they interact (security, UX, and operational constraints), and what the consequences are if they’re missing. It connects multiple concepts (safety, threat modeling, API error handling, and privacy) and tests implications and trade-offs, so it meets the criteria for a high-quality learning question."}

{"vote":"keep","learning_quality_score":8,"vote_reasoning":"This question requires applied troubleshooting and causal reasoning rather than rote recall. It asks students to sequence checks (config syntax, absolute path, build/run, full restart, logs) and to explain why an absolute launch path is required — testing understanding of process discovery, path resolution, process lifecycle, and how stdout/stderr/logs affect inter-process transport. Correct answers demonstrate mental models about how the host locates and spawns servers, why configuration is read only at startup, and how logs reveal runtime/launch failures, which qualifies as a strong conceptual learning item (score 8)."}

{"vote":"keep","learning_quality_score":8,"vote_reasoning":"This question requires diagnosing real-world failure modes of an external API and designing appropriate mitigations (input validation, retries/backoff, rate-limit handling, monitoring, and user messaging). Answering it correctly demonstrates causal understanding of why those failures occur and how system design choices reduce risk — it tests \"why/how\" and connects operational, API, and UX concerns rather than asking for rote facts. Score 8: a strong learning question that probes implications and practical application."}
